# Etsy Integration — Case study 1440 × auto✓ Ready for dev← Back to Portfolio 2026

    





  
Case Study · Product Redesign · 2024–25

  ◆ Built for Shopify
  
Etsy Integration App Redesign

  
A full UX redesign of the Etsy Integration app for Shopify. The app could do a lot, but merchants found it hard to use, so I rebuilt it around the tasks they do every day.

  
Role
Product Designer
Platform
Shopify Ecosystem
System
Polaris v12
Scope
Full UX Overhaul
Team
Sr. Designer · BA · Devs · PO

  Visit app ↗
  




01 : Overview
What is the Etsy Integration App?


The app connects a merchant’s Etsy store to their Shopify store. It keeps inventory in sync, publishes products, manages listings, tracks orders and maps prices and variations between the two.


  • ⇄Sync inventory across both platforms (Etsy - Shopify)
  • ▤Publish and manage product listings
  • ◎Track orders in a unified view
  • ¤Handle pricing & variation mapping
  • ⚙Automate cross-platform workflows



02 : Problem
The features were there. Using them was hard.


The app worked, but years of quick additions had left UX problems on almost every screen.


Features had been added one by one, and nobody had shaped how they fit together. The real gap was the structure of the experience.


Symptoms
  • No clear path through the app
  • Technical language instead of user language
  • Poor hierarchy & action prioritisation
  • Weak information architecture
  • Limited design system consistency
  • Settings-heavy interaction modal


Business impact
  • Delayed time-to-value for new users
  • Low activation confidence at signup
  • Friction in daily merchant workflows
  • High churn risk after onboarding
  • Increased support ticket volume
  • Stalled merchant growth & retention



03 : UX Audit
Where it went wrong


Before designing anything, I audited every major screen and looked at how the screens worked together, not just one page at a time.


  1. InsightResearch: Stakeholder & User Interviews
  2. AuditMethods: Heuristic, Funnel Analysis
  3. StrategySynthesis: Competitive & Flow Mapping
  4. ActionOutput: Categorised Findings & Redesign Briefs


Key audit findings




F-01CriticalBlocking onboarding step
Product import forced users to wait 5–15 min before accessing the app, causing immediate abandonment.


F-02CriticalMandatory product profiling
Users had to sort products into categories by hand before getting any value. It took real effort and gave nothing back right away.


F-03High16-item navigation
Navigation contained 16 items across 3 groups including redundant, rarely-used, and misplaced entries.


F-04HighNon-Polaris UI
Custom sidebar and components broke visual consistency with Shopify admin, reducing merchant trust.


F-05MediumMerchant-hostile language
Technical jargon ("sync interval", "attribute mapping") used throughout without explanation.


F-06MediumNo progressive disclosure
All settings surfaces loaded at once, overwhelming new users before they understood core value.





04 : Define
Four principles we designed by


I turned the research into four principles. Whenever the team had to make a call on a screen, an annotation or a trade-off, we checked it against these.




01Value before configuration
Show merchants what the app does for them before asking them to set anything up. If they wait a long time before seeing any value, that’s a problem we should fix.


02Progressive disclosure
Show only what the user needs for the task in front of them. Advanced and edge-case settings sit one level deeper, so they don’t crowd the main flow.


03Use the merchant’s words
Write labels the way merchants talk: "Sync my products to Etsy", not "Configure variant attribute mapping". Clear words make people as confident as a clear layout does.


04Stay close to Polaris
Following Polaris v12 closely makes the app feel like part of Shopify. Every custom pattern we add is one more thing to maintain and explain later.





05 : Solution
Solution 1: Onboarding flow


The old onboarding had 3 steps and lost a lot of merchants. The steps made sense on paper, but two of them made people wait or do heavy manual work before they could even open the app. We kept 3 steps and changed what each one asks for.


Before
3 steps, high churn
    

  1. Connect Etsy
    OAuth connection to the merchant's Etsy store.
    1 min · manageable
    2. 

  2. Product importing
    Users sat on a loading screen while every Etsy product imported, one at a time. Merchants with large catalogues (500–2,000+ listings) waited 5 to 15 minutes and couldn’t skip ahead.
    Up to 15 min blocked wait · majority abandoned
    3. 

  3. Product profiling
    Anyone who got past step 2 then had to sort their products into Etsy categories by hand before entering the app. It was slow and repetitive, and they still hadn’t seen any value.
    15–30 min manual task · users who reached this still churned


After
3 steps, under 2 minutes
    

  1. Connect Etsy
    The same OAuth step, now with a progress indicator so merchants know what comes next.
    1 min · manageable
    2. 

  2. Choose pricing plan
    A simple comparison of 3 plans, each with a 14-day free trial. Products now import in the background, so nobody waits on a loading screen.
    Choose a plan in under 30 sec
    3. 

  3. Mandatory settings
    Only the settings we need up front: sync frequency and listing defaults. Profiling moved out of onboarding, and merchants can do it inside the app when they need to.
    Setup completed in under 45 sec



Solution 2: Polaris embedded navigation


The old app had its own sidebar with 12+ items, icon rows and grouped sections (SUPPORT, SERVICES) that sat outside the Shopify admin. We replaced it with Polaris’s embedded app navigation, which is one flat list of menu items inside the Shopify admin.


Constraint: Polaris allows only one menu level. That made us decide what really mattered, and the structure got clearer because of it.





06 : Key Screens
Redesigned core screens







07 : Impact
Outcomes & what changed


Awarded the ◆ Built for Shopify badge


After the redesign, the app earned Shopify’s Built for Shopify certification. Shopify gives it only to apps that meet strict standards for performance, UX and Polaris integration. Fewer than 1% of apps in the Shopify App Store have it.



The numbers


40% ↑Onboarding completion rate
32% ↓Support ticket volume
2.8×Dev handoff speed
4.6 ⭐App store rating (from 3.9)



08 : Learnings
Skills & responsibilities


Design skills
  • UX Audit
  • IA Restructuring
  • Workflow Optimisation
  • Microcopy
  • Cognitive load reduction
  • Polaris Design system


Strategic skills
  • System Thinking
  • Business Alignment
  • Cross-functional Collab
  • Stakeholder Comments
  • Dev Handoff & Quality Analysis
  • Scalability-first design


  1. Audited the existing product screen by screen
  2. Reorganised the navigation and grouped related features
  3. Designed all screens from onboarding through listing management
  4. Wrote interaction logic and microcopy across all flows
  5. Collaborated daily with BA and development team
  6. Ensured full Shopify Polaris design system compliance
  7. Presented design solutions and rationale to stakeholders
  8. Supported developer handoff and participated in QA reviews


Thank you!

# Ounce 3.0 — Case study 1440 × auto✓ Ready for dev← Back to Portfolio 2026

    





  
Case Study · Design System · 2023–24

  
Ounce 3.0

  
Ounce is the design system behind our products. I helped rebuild it from scattered, hand-made UI into one documented library that designers and developers both use.

  

    
Role
Product Designer

    
Company
CEDCOSS Technologies

    
Timeline
2023 – 2024

    
Collaborators
Designers, devs, QA, PMs

    
Tools
Figma

  

  

    Button / Primary / LPrimary
    Notifications
    ✓Remember meActive
    45+ components
    Primary · Success · Warning · Danger
    AaType scale
  






  
00 · At a glance

  

    
45+reusable components, covering every type, state and size

    
4pillars: style guide, components, content, docs

    
4product teams aligned on one visual language

    
0relearning needed by end users

  






  
01 · The challenge

  
Every project started from zero.

  
Every new project, and sometimes every new stage of a project, meant redesigning the same components. Their style drifted each time to suit the feature, so designs didn’t match, effort was wasted and teams found it hard to work together.

  

    
01No colour styles
Designers had no defined colour styles to follow, so errors were likely in every file.

    
02A rigid sidebar
Navigation items couldn’t be adjusted. Every change was manual, costing time and resources.

    
03No component library
Size, padding, icon, label, colour, state and type were set by hand on every single button.

    
04Manual data tables
Our most-used element, but columns were undefined and making it responsive was manual.

  

  
We needed to
  • Recreate the old components on a shared, scalable foundation
  • Gather every old use case and define use cases for each component
  • Address executive concerns and adoption difficulties up front






  
02 · Purpose

  
What Ounce 3.0 had to do

  
    
    
  • /01Establish consistencyQuality
    • 
    
  • /02Streamline design & developmentSpeed
    • 
    
  • /03Keep one brand identityBrand
    • 
    
  • /04Scale and adapt with the businessGrowth
    • 
    
  • /05Move from outdated to modern UICraft
    • 
  






  
03 · Process

  
Research, align, build, document

  
The whole team built a component list from what our projects had in common and what future projects would need. Building the library took a lot of time, so we were careful about what went in.

  
    
    
  1. 01 · AuditCollected every old use case and ran UX research on each component.
    2. 
    
  2. 02 · BenchmarkStudied mature design systems for structure, naming and documentation.
    3. 
    
  3. 03 · FoundationsDefined typography, colour styles, icons, spacing and grids.
    4. 
    
  4. 04 · ComponentsBuilt variant-driven components and documented their states and limits.
    5. 
  

  
What the team said in workshops

  

    
S
The sceptic
“We can stay consistent without a formal system, and it might limit our creativity.”

    
D
Developer
“It makes my job easier. I know what to expect and can focus on the technical side.”

    
D
Designer
“It has to be flexible enough for different styles and ideas.”

  

  
Several rounds of stakeholder discussion led to one principle: flexible variants, not rigid templates. Teams get consistency and still have room to be creative.








  

    
04 Before → After

    
What changed, piece by piece

    
Four of the biggest pain points, and how the system fixed them. Click any screenshot to zoom in.


    

      
      
      
      
    


    

      
Before
No defined colour styles. Designers picked from a long list of raw hex values, so going off track was easy and errors were likely.
Raw hex values · no names or roles

      
After
Named, semantic colour styles for every element and component, organised as Primary, Shades, Success, Warning and Danger, plus button-state tokens.
Semantic tokens · Primary/P900 · Shades/G450 · Danger/R300

    

    

      
Before
A static sidebar frame with no flexibility. Every change to items, icons or states was manual.
Static frame · edited by hand

      
After
One sidebar component. The logo, account switcher, logout, menu items, nested items and icons are all controlled from its properties.
Component · Sidebar style variants · item toggles

    

    

      
Before
Buttons were detached shapes. Size, padding, icon, label, colour, state and type were set by hand on each one, so consistency broke easily.
Manual styling · inconsistent spacing

      
After
A button instance with auto layout (Fill × Hug) and colour tokens. Drag it in and configure any case from its properties. It's one of 45+ components.
Auto layout · tokenised · variant-driven

    

    

      
Before
Our most-used element, but rows were built by hand, columns were undefined and making the table responsive was manual.
Hand-built rows · undefined columns

      
After
Built from a Table Cell component with data variants, states and fill-width columns, so the table resizes on its own.
Table Cell component · Fill × 72 · data atoms

    

  








  
05 · The system

  
Four parts, one library

  

    
iStyle Guide
  • Colours
  • Typography
  • Icons & illustrations
  • Grids & layout

    
iiComponent Library
  • Buttons & inputs
  • Alerts & badges
  • Data tables
  • 45+ components

    
iiiContent Guide
  • Principles
  • Definitions
  • Use cases
  • Limitations

    
ivDocumentation
  • Best practices
  • Do’s & don’ts
  • Editorial guidelines
  • Implementation guide

  






  
06 · Component deep-dive

  
Every type, every state

  
A live recreation of the component specs. Switch states to see how each variant responds.

  

    
❖ Button · 7 types × 5 states × 3 sizes

Tip: the controls in the Default row can be clicked






  
★ Key design decision

    
New look, same experience.

    
We deliberately kept the existing interaction patterns and flows, and rebuilt only the visual layer and its consistency. Users needed no relearning, which made the system easier to adopt and lowered the risk of rolling it out.






  
07 · Impact

  
Slow to start, faster after

  
A design system takes more work at the start. Once the library exists, each project gets faster. Without one, speed stays flat for a while and then drops.

  

    

      
Productivity over timeWith system Without

      
    

    
    
      
  • ⚡
    Faster design
    Drag in a configured component instead of rebuilding it.
    • 
      
  • ⇄
    Smoother handoff
    Developers know what to expect and can focus on engineering.
    • 
      
  • ◎
    Consistent across teams
    Four product teams stay aligned across products and platforms.
    • 
      
  • ↗
    Future-proof
    New features plug in without costly redesigns or rework.
    • 
    

  






  
08 · Reflection

  
What I took away

  

    
i.Treat it as a product
A design system needs users, a roadmap and upkeep. It isn’t finished at launch.

    
ii.Align before pixels
Bringing out the sceptics’ concerns early shaped the flexible, variant-first approach and made adoption easier.

    
iii.Docs are the product
Components only scale when their principles, use cases and limits are written down.

  

  
Thanks for reading!
